questions.question: Which statement best describes YARN's core separation of responsibility?
options: The ResourceManager runs every task and stores every data block
The ResourceManager arbitrates cluster resources, while each application's ApplicationMaster coordinates its own work
Each NodeManager decides queue guarantees for the whole cluster
Every container is a permanent virtual machine
questions.explanation: YARN separates global resource arbitration from framework-specific execution. The ResourceManager allocates containers; the ApplicationMaster requests them and tracks that application's tasks.

questions.question: A worker exposes 54 GiB of usable YARN memory and 15 schedulable vcores. Each container requests 6 GiB and 2 vcores. How many containers fit on the node?
questions.explanation: Memory permits floor(54 / 6) = 9 containers, while vcores permit floor(15 / 2) = 7. Both resources must fit, so vcores bind at 7 containers.

questions.question: A cluster can run 120 containers, one queue receives a 40% share, and a stage has 130 equal tasks. Ignoring other overhead, how many execution waves are required?
questions.explanation: The queue receives floor(120 x 0.40) = 48 concurrent containers. ceil(130 / 48) = 3 waves.

questions.question: What is the production meaning of CapacityScheduler elasticity with preemption?
options: A queue may borrow idle capacity, but some borrowed containers can later be reclaimed when another queue needs its guarantee
Every queue always receives its maximum capacity
Preemption permanently deletes the application
Idle capacity must remain unused
questions.explanation: Elastic sharing improves utilization, while preemption can restore guarantees under contention. Applications must tolerate selected containers being stopped and retried.

questions.question: Why can strict node-local placement make a YARN job slower?
options: Node-local reads always cross more racks
Waiting indefinitely for one preferred node can leave suitable containers idle elsewhere
Locality disables queue limits
Node-local tasks cannot use memory
questions.explanation: Locality avoids network reads, but it is a preference with a delay budget. The scheduler eventually relaxes node-local to rack-local or off-switch placement to avoid idle capacity.

questions.question: The active ResourceManager fails while workers and ApplicationMasters are still running. What is the correct first recovery boundary?
options: Delete every application and resubmit it
Promote a standby ResourceManager backed by persisted state and reconstruct cluster state
Increase every container's memory
Reformat the workers' local disks
questions.explanation: The ResourceManager owns cluster-wide scheduling authority. HA and a durable state store restore that control plane; work-preserving recovery can reconstruct live containers from NodeManagers and requests from ApplicationMasters.

questions.question: A worker is lost after a task commits an external side effect but before the ApplicationMaster records completion. What application property contains the retry risk?
options: A larger ResourceManager heap
An idempotent task or output-commit protocol keyed by stable work identity
A lower queue capacity
Disabling log aggregation
questions.explanation: A replacement attempt may replay work after an uncertain outcome. YARN can replace the container, but only the application can make repeated external effects safe.

questions.question: When is YARN usually the strongest platform fit today?
options: Any new stateless web service regardless of its data path
An established Hadoop estate where HDFS locality, YARN-integrated engines, shared queues, and existing operational controls still matter
A single laptop script with no shared resources
A mobile application runtime
questions.explanation: YARN remains current and maintained, but platform choice should follow the workload and operating model. Its strongest fit is commonly an existing Hadoop data platform with locality-sensitive engines and mature YARN controls.
